docs.title: Triton From First Principles
docs.text:
Building Production GPU Kernels in OpenAI Triton, One Layer at a Time

Scope and testing status

All 22 chapters are present. Existing example outputs are interpreter references, not GPU benchmark records. This edition adds original SVGs and an offline technical review; 12 compiled H100 smoke cases have now passed, and all 84 complete references exited zero in interpreter mode. Full compiled chapter coverage remains pending. See the dated execution record and review record.

"A kernel is not finished when it computes the right answer once. It is finished when you can tell the compiler exactly which memory it may touch, which values it may assume never change, and how many threads get to look at each byte at the same time — and PyTorch's own autograd engine can still find its way through it."

This is a practitioner's guide to OpenAI Triton — the Python-embedded language for writing GPU kernels that compile down to machine code competitive with hand-tuned CUDA, without leaving Python. Unlike a systems language building its own tensor library from scratch, Triton is deliberately narrow: it owns the kernel, not the tensor, the device, or the autograd graph. Those belong to PyTorch. The running project in this book is a set of fused, production-style Triton kernels — element-wise ops, a blocked matmul, reductions, fused layer-norm and softmax, attention and top-2 MoE gating — with dedicated chapters wiring custom operations into PyTorch's torch.autograd.Function machinery rather than a hand-rolled graph, and each one pointed, in the closing part, at the same quantitative-finance problems the Mojo book ends on.

No Mojo book is required: comparisons to it are optional analogies, and the Triton concepts are explained here.

The design principles carried through the whole book:

  • Kernel-first, not framework-first. Triton doesn't give you a tensor class or a computational graph — it gives you a compiler for the innermost loop. This book treats that boundary honestly instead of papering over it.
  • PyTorch does the bookkeeping. The autograd chapters wrap custom kernels in torch.autograd.Function, so the chain rule, the graph traversal, and gradient accumulation are the real engine's job, not a toy reimplementation of it.
  • Numbers you can check by hand. Every worked example traces the arithmetic — block indices, strides, masked lanes — before showing the code that produces it.
  • Financial computing examples. The closing chapter compares teaching implementations of Black–Scholes pricing, rolling return statistics, and Monte Carlo option pricing; production use requires additional numerical, domain and GPU validation.

  • 22 chapters

    Part 0 through Part 7, from @triton.jit to Monte Carlo pricing.

  • Real, runnable kernels

    84 complete downloadable reference listings accompany the explanations. Historical interpreter outputs and pending GPU tests are distinguished.

  • 4 appendices

    Setup, a self-check quiz, PyTorch integration and memory-model notes.

  • Real financial models

    Black–Scholes, rolling volatility and Monte Carlo teaching kernels.

docs.title: How the book is organized
docs.text:
Part Focus Part 0 — Triton Foundations Triton's type system and the JIT boundary, kernel parameterization (constexpr, configs), strides and pointers, the grid/program/block model, block-level SPMD vectorization Part 1 — Kernel–Tensor Interface The pointer+stride contract with torch.Tensor, broadcasting and block pointers, GPU-side construction, mask/structure kernels (causal, diagonal, block-sparse), targeting hardware, shared memory and the kernel cache Part 2 — Core Kernels Element-wise kernels, the blocked matmul kernel, reduction kernels Part 3 — Wiring Into PyTorch's Autograd torch.autograd.Function as the real graph node a Triton kernel plugs into Part 4 — The Backward Kernel Writing the backward kernel and ctx.save_for_backward, how PyTorch's autograd engine chains custom ops Part 5 — GPU Acceleration and Performance Autotuning (num_warps, num_stages, BLOCK_SIZE), benchmarking correctly with triton.testing.do_bench Part 6 — Neural Network Building Blocks Fused LayerNorm/softmax/matmul+bias+activation, Flash Attention, top-2 MoE gating and the boundary to a full expert-dispatch system Part 7 — Financial Computing Applications Black–Scholes calls, rolling standard deviation and Monte Carlo call pricing

Start with Getting Started to stand up a Triton + PyTorch + CUDA environment, or jump straight into Part 0: Triton Foundations if your toolchain is already installed.

How this book differs from its Mojo sibling

Triton has no user-defined structs, no hand-built tensor class, and no computational graph of its own — a kernel receives raw pointers and strides, and the tensor, the device, and the autograd graph all belong to PyTorch. Rather than mechanically porting chapters that assume a from-scratch systems language, several parts of this book are deliberately redesigned around what Triton actually is: a compiler for the innermost loop that plugs into a real, existing autograd engine. Parts 3 and 4 in particular trade "build your own AD framework" for "build production-grade fused kernels that plug into PyTorch's real one" — which is what Triton is used for in practice.

docs.title: Complete chapter references: interpreter rerun
docs.text:
All 84 complete reference files at the captured commit exited zero under TRITON_INTERPRET=1 on the same host. They used CPU tensors/interpreter semantics; this count is not 84 GPU-compiled programs. Several files intentionally print negative comparisons to demonstrate bugs. A zero process exit is not proof of all numerical paths. Full source hashes, commands, UTC start/finish times, exit codes and unchanged logs are in the 84-file results index.

The runner used four independent processes with CPU math thread counts set to one; CUDA visibility was GPU 1. Its complete source is retained. Each result's log path is relative to the interpreter/ directory. Historical printed chapter outputs remain historical; these new logs record the captured source identities without editing those earlier outputs. After the final review, 83 sources remain byte-identical; one finance file changes only an incorrect printed maturity label. That exact before/after change is pinned and checked separately; the new label has not been rerun. See the final review.

docs.title: What remains
docs.text: Port and test each chapter's device allocations and physical tile shapes before claiming full compiled-GPU coverage. Backward/gradient correctness, sanitizer coverage, broader dtypes/layouts, performance and the selected fresh-install package target still need dedicated validation. No additional rented GPU is needed to finish publishing this evidence.

docs.title: Final adversarial review — November 21, 2026
docs.text: Three independent reviewers challenged the foundation chapters and installation, the advanced kernels and worked answers, and the illustrations and teaching flow. A follow-up checked the corrections. This is an offline technical review, not a new GPU run or a proof that every possible input is supported.

docs.title: Confirmed issues corrected
docs.text:
Area Correction JIT evidence Interpreter dtype messages no longer claim observed GPU compilations or cache entries. Invalid accesses Removed guarantees that out-of-bounds reads silently succeed; they may fault, corrupt data or appear successful. Memory accounting Distinguished the AoS model's 28-sector union footprint from 112 sector requests across four field instructions; actual DRAM traffic needs measurement. Masking False memory-access lanes do not perform loads/stores; whole-block skipping additionally avoids instructions and address work. Alignment hints Explained contiguous groups and group-start divisibility in Chapter 7 and Appendix D. Floating point FP32 accumulation also rounds; reduction order, K and inputs affect error. Online-softmax identities are exact in real arithmetic, not rounding-free implementations. Autograd Added the first wrappers' small contiguous-FP32 contract and distinguished derivative support from graph capture. Autotuning Added repeated-execution and reset/restore guidance, a mutable-output walkthrough, and compiled-candidate correctness checks. Interpreter equality is scoped to the shown elementwise example. LayerNorm and attention Scoped the one-program-row design; attention query tiles maintain independent state rather than synchronizing programs. MoE Moved the normalized-top2 policy contract before the lesson; other weight policies are not universally wrong. Finance Corrected N(d1)/N(d2), error/maturity attribution and sample-variance versus standard-deviation terminology; distinguished deterministic fixed-draw checks from statistical price comparisons. PyTorch integration Supported direct Triton launches can be captured by torch.compile; registration is an additional integration route rather than a universal prerequisite. Memory appendix Separated register pressure from spilling, qualified dot lowering/staging, added descriptor prerequisites and scoped version-specific warnings. Teaching flow Removed an absent dropout promise, corrected cross-references, made Mojo comparisons optional and moved the long homepage walkthrough after the introduction. Illustrations Corrected the gradient banner's forward/derivative notation; added four appendix banners and four explanatory SVGs. All 55 figures have embedded fonts and checked labels.

Primary references used to resolve the disputed contracts: Triton debugging, NVIDIA memory accesses, alignment, contiguity, autotuning, descriptors, PyTorch direct-launch integration, and the Black–Scholes derivation.

docs.title: Evidence preserved and remaining validation
docs.text:
No numerical kernel operations changed in this review. One complete finance file changes only a misleading printed label: the largest relative error in its example belongs to the first T=1 contract, not the longest T=2 contract. The archived source and raw log remain exact. The source-transition manifest pins both hashes; the verifier permits exactly that single print-string replacement and rejects additional changes. The corrected label itself has not been rerun.

The November 21 record still contains 12 passing compiled H100 smoke cases and 84 zero-exit interpreter captures. Eighty-three captured reference sources remain byte-identical; one has the label-only revision above. The appendix snippets were not among those 84 files and have not been rerun on that host. Full compiled chapter coverage, appendix execution, backward GPU validation, broader inputs, sanitizer coverage and performance testing remain separate work. A new GPU is not required for these prose, diagram and label fixes.

docs.title: Offline validation
docs.text:
• 84 complete current listings parse and match their downloadable sources.
  • Ten independent CPU arithmetic tests cover the worked examples, sector counting and finance attribution.
  • Three evidence regression tests reject source drift and edited captured logs.
  • All 55 SVGs pass XML, embedded-font, glyph, bounds and label-overlap checks.
  • Strict MkDocs build and built internal-link/fragment checks pass.

Historical outputs are not edited to match new wording, and no verifier is disabled to obtain a successful build. The review found no new critical numerical-kernel issue within the stated examples; its scope does not certify untested contracts.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Start by choosing an execution mode. Reading, building the website and checking Python syntax need no GPU. Interpreter references need a supported Linux Python/Triton installation but do not compile GPU code. Real kernel correctness and performance need a compatible NVIDIA GPU and working driver.

The book contains 22 chapters. Its older printed results are author-reported interpreter outputs, not dated GPU captures. This review has not converted them into GPU results. See the review and testing record for what was checked and what remains pending.

docs.title: 1 — Inspect a managed GPU host before installing anything
docs.text:
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release
nvidia-smi
python3 --version

An H100 or GH200 is suitable for the planned single-GPU tests. GH200 uses an ARM64 CPU (aarch64); ordinary H100 hosts commonly use x86_64. Select wheels and system packages for the actual CPU architecture. Apple Silicon's ARM CPU does not make macOS a CUDA/Triton GPU platform. Windows users should use a supported Linux/WSL GPU setup rather than assuming native Linux wheels work on Windows.

Keep a working provider driver. nvidia-smi checks the driver/device path; it does not prove that PyTorch is CUDA-enabled, that Triton can compile, or that a kernel is correct. A missing nvcc is not by itself a failure: normal wheel-based PyTorch/Triton use does not require installing the complete CUDA C++ toolkit. CUDA extensions and profiling tools have separate requirements.

docs.title: 2 — Fresh Ubuntu 24.04: host prerequisites
docs.text:
On a new host, install the Python environment and host compiler tools:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y python3-venv python3-dev build-essential git ca-certificates wget

If a physical x86-64 Ubuntu 24.04 machine has no working NVIDIA driver, NVIDIA's network repository path is:

sudo apt-get install -y linux-headers-$(uname -r)
wget https://developer.download.nvidia.com/compute/cuda/repos/ubuntu2404/x86_64/cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb
sudo dpkg -i cuda-keyring_1.1-1_all.deb
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-open
sudo reboot

Reconnect after reboot and repeat nvidia-smi. Follow any required Secure Boot module-enrollment instructions. These commands are for the stated OS/architecture, not a prescription to replace a working cloud stack. For GH200/ARM64, use the provider's supported image and the matching NVIDIA SBSA/ARM installation procedure; do not install x86-64 driver repositories. See NVIDIA's driver installation guide for platform-specific prerequisites and packages. This offline review did not perform a fresh bare-metal driver installation.

docs.title: 3 — Create an isolated runtime environment
docs.text:
The selected reproducibility target is PyTorch 2.9.1 with CUDA 12.8 wheels and Triton 3.5.1, not a claim that every chapter has already been GPU-tested with it. Official indexes provide Linux x86-64 and ARM64 wheels. Python 3.12 on Ubuntu 24.04 is a straightforward choice.

python3 -m venv .venv-runtime
source .venv-runtime/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install 'torch==2.9.1' --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128
python -m pip install 'triton==3.5.1' numpy scipy pandas
python -m pip check

The explicit Triton version matches this PyTorch release's x86-64 dependency; it also avoids assuming the same dependency marker installs Triton on ARM64. Do not upgrade Triton independently and assume compatibility remains established. Preserve an existing supported provider environment if appropriate, recording its exact versions instead.

Sources: official PyTorch CUDA wheel index, PyTorch 2.9.1 metadata, Triton 3.5.1 wheels. The wheel's CUDA runtime and the installed driver are separate components; the host driver must support the selected runtime and generated GPU code.

docs.title: 4 — Run a real GPU smoke test
docs.text:
Clone the book, then use its complete GPU smoke test source:

git clone https://github.com/MaximumBeings/triton-from-first-principles.git
cd triton-from-first-principles
unset TRITON_INTERPRET
python docs/examples/gpu_smoke.py

The script refuses interpreter mode and a missing CUDA device. It checks a masked strided vector operation, ragged GEMM and causal/non-causal attention against independent CPU references. It uses supported physical dot tile extents and explicit FP32 precision. All twelve GPU smoke cases passed on H100 on November 21, 2026, using the provider’s PyTorch 2.7.0/Triton 3.3.0 stack. See the captured output, exact dates and source hash. This does not validate the separate installation target or every chapter on the compiled backend.

The hand-sized BLOCK=4 dot examples elsewhere deliberately trace interpreter arithmetic. They cannot simply be launched on the NVIDIA compiled backend unchanged. CUDA allocation, valid physical tile shapes and the specified dtype/precision contract all matter.

docs.title: 5 — Reproduce an interpreter reference separately
docs.text:
Download a chapter's complete file and use its printed interpreter command:

TRITON_INTERPRET=1 python chapter_reference.py

Set the variable before importing Triton. The interpreter bypasses compilation and simulates program instances sequentially; it is not GPU emulation. CPU results do not prove supported dot tile shapes, races, alignment assumptions, resource use, or performance. Triton's debugging guide explains the limits.

docs.title: 6 — Build the website without GPU dependencies
docs.text:
Use a separate environment so documentation work does not replace runtime packages:

python3 -m venv .venv-docs
source .venv-docs/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python tools/verify_book.py
python tools/verify_svg_readability.py
mkdocs build --strict
python tools/verify_site_links.py
mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000. Clicking diagrams opens an accessible overlay on the chapter; Escape, Close and Back dismiss it. Fit width preserves readable type with vertical scrolling; Fit whole shows the entire figure.

docs.title: 7 — Save evidence before releasing a rented host
docs.text:
Record the real device/driver, CPU architecture, Python/PyTorch/Triton versions, source hashes, exact commands, UTC start/finish times, exit codes and raw output. Save python -m pip freeze and nvidia-smi -q. Separate interpreter checks, actual GPU kernels and benchmarks. A process that merely exits zero after reporting an unavailable driver is not a passing GPU test.

See Appendix A for troubleshooting.

docs.title: Technical Review and Testing Status
docs.text:
Review date: November 21, 2026. This pass reviewed technical contracts, source listings, installation instructions and diagrams without a CUDA host. A subsequent H100 session passed 12 compiled smoke cases and reran all 84 complete references in interpreter mode. This does not establish full compiled-GPU coverage; see the dated execution record.

See also the final adversarial review and corrections.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text: Area Correction Homepage Replaced the obsolete “only Chapter 1 exists” notice; listed the actual 22 chapters and four appendices; removed promises of absent grouped expert GEMM, bond/credit/duration implementations and universal autograd coverage. JIT/cache Pointer arguments do not automatically specialize on tensor shape. Corrected the claimed meaning of interpreter static_print messages and distinguished specialization keys from final instruction equality. GPU resources BLOCK is a logical tile extent, not a register count in one thread. Corrected the BLOCK=65536 explanation, staging-knob guarantees and classic-language versus experimental API scope. Matrix operations Marked hand-sized dot tiles as interpreter-specific. FP32 teaching dots now explicitly request IEEE input precision; their previous interpreter outputs are not GPU results. Attention Replaced loop-continue control flow with a bounded causal loop, documented physical tile limits and top-left masking, and qualified numerical, tie, all-masked-row and MoE gating contracts. Top-k Removed the blanket assertion that Triton has no built-in top-k; linked the modern API and distinguished this hand-built value/index selection. Autograd Flat-address GELU wrappers now make inputs/upstream gradients contiguous. Documented first-order scope and the need for a separate higher-order implementation. Finance Distinguished N(d1) from risk-neutral exercise probability N(d2), added domain/zero-boundary requirements, and explained variance and Monte Carlo conventions. Installation Selected a documented PyTorch 2.9.1/cu128 + Triton 3.5.1 target, addressed ARM64 separately, preserved provider drivers and separated documentation dependencies from GPU dependencies. This target has not been GPU-tested in this pass. Reader experience Added 55 original embedded-font SVGs (22 chapter banners, two entry-page banners, four appendix banners and 27 worked/overview figures), chapter-level download links, a worked quiz and a same-page viewer with fit-width/fit-whole controls and navigation cleanup.

docs.title: Offline checks and their limits
docs.text:
All 84 explicitly titled complete Python reference listings parse and have byte-identical downloads with recorded hashes. The new GPU-smoke source also passes Python syntax checks. Syntax parsing does not import PyTorch/Triton, compile a GPU kernel or execute its mathematics.

Ten CPU binary64 tests check the worked stride/mask/GEMM/GELU/softmax/variance/option/payoff arithmetic. SVG checks examine embedded fonts, glyph coverage, label bounds and overlap. A strict documentation build and built-link check cover page structure and targets. These checks are not a substitute for interpreter reruns, GPU numerical tests, sanitizer checks or benchmarking.

The original source-identity inventory records the pre-review baseline. Historical outputs already printed in the chapters remain author-reported interpreter results. The repository did not supply their original raw logs, package snapshots or per-run timestamps. This review does not invent that historical evidence. A separate interpreter rerun records the captured source hashes and fresh logs. A later print-label-only correction in one finance file is explicitly pinned; its revised label has not been recaptured. No numerical operations changed. Current downloads identify current source; a historical printed result is not a new validation of its hash.

docs.title: First GPU validation and remaining work
docs.text:
The complete new NVIDIA smoke source was compiled and executed on H100. It allocates CUDA tensors, uses physically valid dot tiles and checks twelve cases: three masked strided additions, three ragged GEMMs and six attention cases against CPU references. All twelve cases passed on November 21. The raw captured output records the actual provider stack and source identity; twelve smoke cases are not the full chapter suite.

An H100 or GH200 is suitable for this single-GPU pass. GH200 needs the matching ARM64 software stack. Ordinary chapter references often allocate CPU tensors or deliberately demonstrate invalid kernels; do not bulk-run them in GPU mode by only unsetting TRITON_INTERPRET. Port and classify each test's contract, including intentional failures, before claiming compiled coverage.

A future capture must include exact source hashes, commands, real CPU/GPU/driver and package versions, UTC execution dates, exit codes and unedited stdout/stderr. Measure performance only on the real GPU and state timing scope. No numerical outputs or timings from a future GPU run are fabricated here.
