mask = offsets < n   -->  programs 0-8: mask is all-True (no effect)
                          program 9:    mask is True for 784 lanes,
                                        False for the remaining 240

[COMMON TRAP] A masked single-input forward kernel (Chapter 9) has exactly one load and one store to get right. This chapter's backward kernel has two independent loads (x, grad_out) that must share the same mask, plus the store — three chances to typo, copy-paste incorrectly, or simply forget. Compute mask = offsets < n once, and pass that identical variable to every tl.load and the final tl.store, rather than re-deriving it (or, worse, omitting it) at each call site.

docs.title: 16.3 [FOUNDATIONAL] Wiring the Real Kernel Into TritonGELU, and Precision in the Backward Pass
Intuition
docs.text:
With a genuinely masked, multi-program backward kernel in hand, replacing Chapter 15's placeholder is almost anticlimactic: TritonGELU.backward already had the right shape — retrieve x from ctx.saved_tensors, compute something from it and grad_output, and return that. All that changes is what "compute something" means: a call into gelu_backward_kernel instead of four lines of torch.erf/torch.exp. The forward staticmethod gets the same treatment, replacing Chapter 15's single-block launch with triton_gelu_forward's masked multi-program version. The autograd machinery Chapter 15 established — ctx.save_for_backward, the resulting TritonGELUBackward graph node, .grad_fn, .backward() — needs no changes at all; it was already correctly built around whatever computation forward and backward perform internally.

The other loose end is precision. Chapter 13.3 showed that accumulating a matmul's inner-product sum in fp16 versus fp32 produces a real, measurable gap. A backward kernel like this one has no accumulation loop — there's nothing being summed across iterations — so that specific lesson doesn't transfer directly. But a related question does: does the storage dtype of the gradient itself matter, independent of what precision the arithmetic runs in? And what happens if the inputs are already fp16, since that's an entirely realistic scenario for a network trained in mixed precision? Both turn out to have real, verifiable answers — one of them genuinely surprising.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Precision question What Chapter 13.3 already established What's new here Where does precision loss come from? Summing many products across loop iterations in a low-precision accumulator An elementwise kernel with no loop — precision loss can only come from the storage dtype of inputs and outputs, not accumulation Does the math library care about input dtype? Not tested tl.math.erf refuses fp16 input outright, raising an error rather than silently computing in reduced precision Fix Accumulate in fp32 regardless of input/output dtype (a Triton/CUDA-wide convention) Explicitly .to(tl.float32) before calling erf/exp, then let the store back to grad_in_ptr cast to whatever dtype the output tensor actually is

docs.title: Worked Example 16.3.1: TritonGELU, fully wired, multi-block forward and backward
docs.text:
class TritonGELU(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        out = triton_gelu_forward(x)
        ctx.save_for_backward(x)
        return out

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        x, = ctx.saved_tensors
        return triton_gelu_backward(grad_output.contiguous(), x)

Run on n = 5000 — large enough to require five separate programs in both directions — genuinely captured:

y.grad_fn: <torch.autograd.function.TritonGELUBackward object at 0x7fcb6784ae00>
forward allclose to oracle?  True
x.grad allclose to oracle?  True
max forward diff: 7.152557373046875e-07
max grad diff:    2.384185791015625e-07

(The exact memory address after object at will differ every run, exactly as Chapter 15 noted — everything else is deterministic.) Both the forward output and the backward gradient now come entirely from genuine Triton kernel launches, masked and multi-program in both directions, and both still agree with PyTorch's own GELU to ordinary floating-point noise.

docs.title: Worked Example 16.3.2: fp16 storage costs precision even when the math runs in fp32
docs.text:
First, the naive attempt — passing fp16 tensors directly into gelu_backward_kernel from Worked Example 16.2.1, unmodified:

InterpreterError: ValueError("Expected dtype ['fp32', 'fp64'] but got fp16")

This is a genuine, immediate failure — not a crash, not silent wrong output, but a caught, informative exception. TRITON_INTERPRET=1 wraps the underlying error in its own InterpreterError, but the message it carries is tl.math.erf's own: a plain ValueError refusing to run erf on an fp16 operand at all. The fix is one explicit cast, added to both loads:

x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)

With that upcast in place, the kernel runs on fp16 tensors without error. But running it, storing both the inputs and the output gradient as genuine fp16 tensors, and comparing against an fp64 ground truth alongside a full-fp32 run of the identical kernel, genuinely captured:

fp32-in/fp32-out max abs diff from fp64 ground truth:   2.360000217471736e-07
fp16-in/fp16-out (fp32 math internally) max abs diff:   0.0015156170082177844
ratio (fp16 path error / fp32 path error):              6422.105375233661

The arithmetic inside the kernel is running in fp32 in both cases — the only difference is that the fp16 version's inputs and output are each rounded to fp16's roughly 3-decimal-digit precision the moment they're loaded and stored. That rounding alone costs a factor of roughly six thousand in accuracy, with no loop, no accumulation, and no difference in the formula whatsoever. Precision loss from storage dtype is a genuinely different mechanism from Chapter 13.3's accumulation-precision loss, and it applies even to the simplest possible elementwise kernel.

docs.title: ASCII Diagram
docs.text:
fp16 tensor in memory          fp32 arithmetic inside kernel         fp16 tensor in memory
 (~3 decimal digits) ---load-->  (full fp32 precision,        --store--> (~3 decimal digits)
                        + .to(fp32)   erf/exp computed exactly)              again

 Rounding happens HERE                                          and HERE
 (on the way in)                                                (on the way out)
 -- regardless of how precisely the math in between was computed.

[COMMON TRAP] It's tempting to assume tl.math.erf will "just work" on fp16 tensors, perhaps at reduced but tolerable precision. What actually happens is a hard ValueError at kernel-launch time — Triton's math library only accepts fp32 or fp64 operands for erf, full stop. Fixing that with an explicit .to(tl.float32) is necessary, but it is not sufficient for full fp32-level accuracy: the fp16 storage of the surrounding tensors still rounds off precision on every load and every store, independent of what precision the arithmetic in between used. Upcasting inside the kernel fixes the crash; it does not fix the storage-precision cost, because that cost was never inside the kernel's math to begin with.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)


@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, d_gelu, mask=mask)  # BUG: never multiplied by grad_out


def section_16_1():
    print("=== Section 16.1: the backward kernel vs. Chapter 15's plain-PyTorch formula ===")
    x = torch.tensor([-1.0, 0.5, 2.0])
    n = x.numel()
    BLOCK = triton.next_power_of_2(n)

    grad_output_ones = torch.ones_like(x)
    x_oracle1 = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    y_oracle1 = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle1, approximate="none")
    y_oracle1.backward(grad_output_ones)

    correct_grad1 = torch.empty_like(x)
    gelu_backward_kernel[(1,)](grad_output_ones, x, correct_grad1, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    buggy_grad1 = torch.empty_like(x)
    gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule[(1,)](grad_output_ones, x, buggy_grad1, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)

    print("with grad_output=1.0 (both look correct):")
    print("  correct kernel matches oracle?", torch.allclose(correct_grad1, x_oracle1.grad))
    print("  buggy kernel matches oracle?  ", torch.allclose(buggy_grad1, x_oracle1.grad))

    grad_output_twos = torch.full_like(x, 2.0)
    x_oracle2 = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    y_oracle2 = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle2, approximate="none")
    y_oracle2.backward(grad_output_twos)

    correct_grad2 = torch.empty_like(x)
    gelu_backward_kernel[(1,)](grad_output_twos, x, correct_grad2, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    buggy_grad2 = torch.empty_like(x)
    gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule[(1,)](grad_output_twos, x, buggy_grad2, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)

    print("with grad_output=2.0 (the trap is exposed):")
    print("  correct kernel matches oracle?", torch.allclose(correct_grad2, x_oracle2.grad))
    print("  buggy kernel matches oracle?  ", torch.allclose(buggy_grad2, x_oracle2.grad))
    print("  buggy kernel is exactly half? ", torch.allclose(buggy_grad2 * 2.0, x_oracle2.grad))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    section_16_1()

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def gelu_forward_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    out = x * cdf
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, out, mask=mask)


@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)


def triton_gelu_forward(x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_forward_kernel[grid](x, out, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return out


def triton_gelu_backward(grad_output, x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    grad_output = grad_output.contiguous()
    grad_input = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_backward_kernel[grid](grad_output, x, grad_input, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return grad_input


def section_16_2():
    print("=== Section 16.2: masked multi-program launch, n=10000, BLOCK=1024 ===")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    n = 10000
    BLOCK = 1024
    print(f"triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK) = {triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK)} programs")

    x = torch.randn(n)
    out = triton_gelu_forward(x, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    oracle_out = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x, approximate="none")
    print("forward allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(out, oracle_out, atol=1e-5))

    grad_output = torch.randn(n)
    grad_input = triton_gelu_backward(grad_output, x, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    x_oracle = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    y_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
    y_oracle.backward(grad_output)
    print("backward allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(grad_input, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    section_16_2()

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def gelu_forward_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    out = x * cdf
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, out, mask=mask)


@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel_upcast(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)


def triton_gelu_forward(x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_forward_kernel[grid](x, out, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return out


def triton_gelu_backward(grad_output, x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    grad_output = grad_output.contiguous()
    grad_input = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_backward_kernel_upcast[grid](grad_output, x, grad_input, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return grad_input


class TritonGELU(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        out = triton_gelu_forward(x)
        ctx.save_for_backward(x)
        return out

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        x, = ctx.saved_tensors
        return triton_gelu_backward(grad_output.contiguous(), x)


def section_16_3():
    print("=== Section 16.3: TritonGELU wired end-to-end, n=5000 ===")
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    n = 5000
    x = torch.randn(n, requires_grad=True)
    y = TritonGELU.apply(x)
    print("y.grad_fn:", y.grad_fn)
    y.sum().backward()

    x_oracle = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    y_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
    y_oracle.sum().backward()

    print("forward allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(y.detach(), y_oracle.detach(), atol=1e-5))
    print("x.grad allclose to oracle? ", torch.allclose(x.grad, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))

    print()
    print("=== Section 16.3: fp16 storage precision vs. fp32, with fp32 math throughout ===")
    torch.manual_seed(2)
    n2 = 2048
    BLOCK2 = 512
    x_fp32 = torch.randn(n2) * 3.0
    grad_out_fp32 = torch.randn(n2)

    x64 = x_fp32.double().requires_grad_(True)
    y64 = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x64, approximate="none")
    y64.backward(grad_out_fp32.double())
    ground_truth = x64.grad

    grad_in_fp32 = triton_gelu_backward(grad_out_fp32, x_fp32, BLOCK=BLOCK2)
    diff_fp32 = (grad_in_fp32.double() - ground_truth).abs().max().item()
    print("fp32-in/fp32-out max abs diff from fp64 ground truth:", diff_fp32)

    x_fp16 = x_fp32.half()
    grad_out_fp16 = grad_out_fp32.half()
    grad_in_fp16 = triton_gelu_backward(grad_out_fp16, x_fp16, BLOCK=BLOCK2)
    diff_fp16 = (grad_in_fp16.double() - ground_truth).abs().max().item()
    print("fp16-in/fp16-out (fp32 math internally) max abs diff:", diff_fp16)
    print("ratio (fp16 path error / fp32 path error):", diff_fp16 / diff_fp32)

    print()
    print("=== Section 16.3: tl.math.erf refuses fp16 operands without the upcast ===")
    try:
        grad_in_bad = torch.empty(n2, dtype=torch.float16)
        grid = (triton.cdiv(n2, BLOCK2),)

        @triton.jit
        def _gelu_backward_no_upcast(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
            pid = tl.program_id(0)
            offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
            mask = offsets < n
            x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
            grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
            SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
            SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
            cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
            pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
            d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
            grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
            tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)

        _gelu_backward_no_upcast[grid](grad_out_fp16, x_fp16, grad_in_bad, n2, BLOCK=BLOCK2)
        print("no exception raised (unexpected)")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"caught exception, as expected: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    section_16_3()

"""
Chapter 16 standalone: writing, generalizing, wiring, and measuring the
precision of a genuine Triton backward kernel for GELU.

Deliberately excludes the mask-omission crash from Worked Example 16.2.2 --
that demonstration kills the process outright (a real, reproducible
segmentation fault under TRITON_INTERPRET=1), so it cannot be safely
combined with the rest of this file's output. See the chapter text for
that demonstration's genuinely captured result, run in isolation.
"""
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 16.1: the backward kernel, and the chain-rule trap
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)


@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, d_gelu, mask=mask)  # BUG: never multiplied by grad_out


def section_16_1():
    print("=== Section 16.1: invisible at grad_output=1, exposed at grad_output=2 ===")
    x = torch.tensor([-1.0, 0.5, 2.0])
    n = x.numel()
    BLOCK = triton.next_power_of_2(n)

    for label, grad_output in [("grad_output=1.0", torch.ones_like(x)),
                                ("grad_output=2.0", torch.full_like(x, 2.0))]:
        x_oracle = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
        y_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
        y_oracle.backward(grad_output)

        correct_grad = torch.empty_like(x)
        gelu_backward_kernel[(1,)](grad_output, x, correct_grad, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
        buggy_grad = torch.empty_like(x)
        gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule[(1,)](grad_output, x, buggy_grad, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)

        print(f"{label}: correct matches oracle? {torch.allclose(correct_grad, x_oracle.grad)}"
              f"  buggy matches oracle? {torch.allclose(buggy_grad, x_oracle.grad)}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 16.2: masked, multi-program generalization
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@triton.jit
def gelu_forward_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    out = x * cdf
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, out, mask=mask)


def triton_gelu_forward(x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_forward_kernel[grid](x, out, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return out


def triton_gelu_backward_plain(grad_output, x, BLOCK=1024):
    grad_input = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_backward_kernel[grid](grad_output, x, grad_input, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return grad_input


def section_16_2():
    print("=== Section 16.2: n=10000, BLOCK=1024, 10 programs (last one masked) ===")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    n = 10000
    BLOCK = 1024
    x = torch.randn(n)
    out = triton_gelu_forward(x, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    oracle_out = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x, approximate="none")
    print("forward allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(out, oracle_out, atol=1e-5))

    grad_output = torch.randn(n)
    grad_input = triton_gelu_backward_plain(grad_output, x, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    x_oracle = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    y_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
    y_oracle.backward(grad_output)
    print("backward allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(grad_input, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Section 16.3: wired into TritonGELU, plus fp16 vs. fp32 storage precision
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel_upcast(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0).to(tl.float32)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)


def triton_gelu_backward(grad_output, x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    grad_output = grad_output.contiguous()
    grad_input = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_backward_kernel_upcast[grid](grad_output, x, grad_input, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return grad_input


class TritonGELU(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        out = triton_gelu_forward(x)
        ctx.save_for_backward(x)
        return out

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        x, = ctx.saved_tensors
        return triton_gelu_backward(grad_output.contiguous(), x)


def section_16_3():
    print("=== Section 16.3: TritonGELU wired end-to-end, n=5000 ===")
    torch.manual_seed(1)
    n = 5000
    x = torch.randn(n, requires_grad=True)
    y = TritonGELU.apply(x)
    y.sum().backward()

    x_oracle = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    y_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
    y_oracle.sum().backward()

    print("forward allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(y.detach(), y_oracle.detach(), atol=1e-5))
    print("x.grad allclose to oracle? ", torch.allclose(x.grad, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))

    print()
    print("=== Section 16.3: fp16 vs. fp32 storage precision (fp32 math throughout) ===")
    torch.manual_seed(2)
    n2, BLOCK2 = 2048, 512
    x_fp32 = torch.randn(n2) * 3.0
    grad_out_fp32 = torch.randn(n2)

    x64 = x_fp32.double().requires_grad_(True)
    y64 = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x64, approximate="none")
    y64.backward(grad_out_fp32.double())
    ground_truth = x64.grad

    grad_in_fp32 = triton_gelu_backward(grad_out_fp32, x_fp32, BLOCK=BLOCK2)
    diff_fp32 = (grad_in_fp32.double() - ground_truth).abs().max().item()
    print("fp32-in/fp32-out max abs diff from fp64 ground truth:", diff_fp32)

    grad_in_fp16 = triton_gelu_backward(grad_out_fp32.half(), x_fp32.half(), BLOCK=BLOCK2)
    diff_fp16 = (grad_in_fp16.double() - ground_truth).abs().max().item()
    print("fp16-in/fp16-out (fp32 math internally) max abs diff:", diff_fp16)
    print("ratio (fp16 path error / fp32 path error):", diff_fp16 / diff_fp32)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    section_16_1()
    print()
    section_16_2()
    print()
    section_16_3()

docs.title: Chapter Summary
docs.text: A backward kernel is not a new kind of Triton program — GELU's derivative, Φ(x) + x*φ(x), is exactly as elementwise as GELU itself, built from the same masked-load-compute-store body as every kernel since Chapter 9 (Section 16.1). What is genuinely new is the chain rule: a correct backward must multiply that local derivative by grad_output, and forgetting that multiplication produces a kernel that passes any test built around .sum().backward() — where grad_output happens to be uniformly 1 — while being silently wrong the moment it sits inside a larger graph receiving a real, non-uniform gradient from upstream. Generalizing Chapter 15's single-block launch into a genuine masked, multi-program grid carried no new arithmetic, only more chances to get the masking wrong across two aligned input loads and one store — and omitting that masking entirely was shown to produce not a subtle wrong number but a real, reproducible crash in this book's own interpreter environment, honestly captured rather than glossed over (Section 16.2). Wiring the resulting kernel into TritonGELU.forward/backward required no changes to the autograd machinery Chapter 15 already built; what it did surface was a genuinely new precision question distinct from Chapter 13.3's accumulation-loop lesson — fp16 storage costs real precision on every load and store regardless of the arithmetic's own precision, and Triton's own tl.math.erf refuses fp16 operands outright rather than silently degrading (Section 16.3).

docs.title: Self-Check Questions
docs.text:
1. Why does gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule (which returns the local derivative d_gelu directly, without multiplying by grad_out) pass a test built on y.sum().backward() but fail on (2 * y).sum().backward()?
  2. Chapter 9's forward masking pattern involves one masked load and one masked store. What is the analogous count for this chapter's backward kernel, and why?
  3. What genuinely happens in this book's environment when both the loads and the store in a multi-program kernel omit mask= entirely, and why is that demonstration deliberately excluded from the chapter's combined 04_standalone_complete.py file?
  4. What changed inside TritonGELU.forward and TritonGELU.backward between Chapter 15 and this chapter, and what, specifically, did not need to change?
  5. Worked Example 16.3.2 ran the exact same fp32 arithmetic (via an explicit .to(tl.float32) upcast) on both the fp32-storage and fp16-storage versions of the kernel, yet the fp16 version was roughly 6,000 times less accurate. If the arithmetic was identical, where did that error actually come from?

docs.title: Where We Go Next
docs.text: TritonGELU now has a genuine Triton kernel on both sides of the chain rule — but it still only knows how to be one, isolated node. Chapter 17 puts it inside an actual multi-operation graph, chaining TritonGELU with ordinary PyTorch operations both before and after it, and examines exactly how PyTorch's autograd engine decides which backward to call, in which order, and how grad_output at each node is actually assembled from whatever the next node downstream produced — the mechanism this chapter's chain-rule trap depended on without yet explaining.

docs.title: Worked Solutions
docs.text:
1. .sum().backward() calls backward with grad_output implicitly equal to a tensor of all 1.0s — under that specific condition, grad_output * d_gelu and d_gelu alone are numerically identical, since multiplying by 1 changes nothing. (2 * y).sum().backward() calls backward with grad_output equal to 2.0 everywhere instead; the correct kernel scales its output by that factor and matches the oracle, while the buggy kernel still returns the untouched local derivative — exactly half the correct answer, as Worked Example 16.1.2 demonstrated directly.
  2. Three: two masked loads (x and grad_out) and one masked store (grad_in), versus the forward kernel's one masked load and one masked store. The backward kernel reads two aligned input tensors instead of one, and both must be indexed and masked identically, or the elements being multiplied together at each lane would come from mismatched positions.
  3. The process crashes outright — a genuine, reproducible segmentation fault (captured as exit code 139), not a Python exception and not a wrong-but-printable number, because the tail program's unmasked load and store reach past the end of every tensor's allocated memory. It is excluded from 04_standalone_complete.py because a hard process crash cannot be safely combined with other code in the same script — it would kill the entire file's execution and destroy every other section's output along with it, which is exactly why the chapter documents it separately, run once, in isolation.
  4. What changed: forward now calls triton_gelu_forward (a genuine masked, multi-program Triton launch) instead of Chapter 15's single-block wrapper, and backward now calls triton_gelu_backward (another genuine masked, multi-program Triton kernel implementing the analytical derivative) instead of four lines of plain torch.erf/torch.exp arithmetic. What did not change: the torch.autograd.Function scaffolding itself — ctx.save_for_backward(x), the @staticmethod structure, and the resulting TritonGELUBackward graph node all work identically regardless of what forward and backward compute internally, because autograd only cares that the two methods exist and are consistent with each other, not what's inside them.
  5. It came entirely from storage, not arithmetic: converting the input to fp16 rounds it to roughly three decimal digits of precision before the load; tl.load reads that already-rounded value, and .to(tl.float32) cannot restore the lost bits, and every tl.store back into an fp16 output tensor rounds the fully-precise fp32 result down to fp16 on the way out. The arithmetic in between ran at full fp32 precision in both versions of the test — the roughly 6,000x accuracy gap is the cost of fp16's limited storage precision alone, a genuinely different mechanism from Chapter 13.3's accumulation-precision loss, which came from summing many low-precision partial products across loop iterations rather than from storing a single value.

docs.title: Backward scope and layout contract
docs.text: The flat-address GELU wrappers make inputs and upstream gradients contiguous before launching. This preserves logical values for transposed or sliced tensors; pointer increments alone do not understand arbitrary PyTorch strides. The custom Triton backward supports first-order gradients. A raw Triton launch does not create a PyTorch graph for that backward, so higher-order derivatives require a differentiable backward or an explicit rejection such as once_differentiable. A first-order comparison or a single .sum().backward() is not a gradgrad test. Fan-in accumulation here describes one backward traversal, not an assertion that a node can never run again in a separate traversal.

docs.title: Chapter 17: How PyTorch's Autograd Engine Chains Custom Ops
docs.text: A custom backward method that has only ever been tested alone has only been tested against the one input it can never actually receive in practice: a grad_output of uniform ones.

docs.title: What you will understand by the end of this chapter
docs.text:
• What grad_output actually looks like when TritonGELU sits inside a real expression — 2 * TritonGELU(x) + 1, not an isolated .sum().backward() — and why it is essentially never uniformly 1 in practice
  • Why Chapter 16's chain-rule bug, which needed a hand-constructed grad_output=2.0 to expose in isolation, shows up on its own the moment TritonGELU is used inside any ordinary multi-operation expression
  • How to read a computation graph directly from PyTorch's own objects — .grad_fn, .grad_fn.next_functions — to see which node points to which, without guessing
  • Why autograd calls backward methods in the reverse of the order their forwards ran, and what "reverse topological order" concretely means for a chain of two custom ops
  • Why a value used by more than one downstream computation causes its producer's backward to be called exactly once, with an already-summed grad_output — not once per consumer — and why a custom backward must never assume grad_output reflects only a single use

docs.title: What you need to know first
docs.text:
• Chapter 15's torch.autograd.Function, ctx.save_for_backward, and how .grad_fn connects an output tensor back to the operation that produced it
  • Chapter 16's real, masked Triton kernels for TritonGELU.forward/backward, and its chain-rule trap — a backward that returns the local derivative without multiplying by grad_output, invisible specifically when grad_output happens to be uniform 1s
  • Chapter 12's oracle-based verification method (torch.nn.functional.gelu, torch.allclose), used throughout this chapter to confirm a multi-operation chain's gradient against PyTorch's own autograd

docs.title: Intuition
docs.text:
Every worked example in Chapters 15 and 16 called .sum().backward() (or .backward() on an explicitly constructed tensor) directly on TritonGELU's own output. That is a reasonable way to isolate and test one operation, but it is not how custom ops get used in practice — a real model calls TritonGELU.apply(x) and then keeps computing with the result: scaling it, adding a bias, feeding it into another layer. The moment that happens, TritonGELU.backward no longer receives grad_output from .sum()'s own gradient (a uniform 1, since d(sum)/d(each element) = 1). It receives whatever the chain rule produces from everything downstream of it — and Chapter 16 already showed exactly what a chain rule multiplication looks like when a coefficient is involved.

This means Chapter 16's chain-rule trap wasn't a contrived edge case that needed an artificially scaled grad_output to expose — that scaling is just what an ordinary multiplication downstream looks like from TritonGELU's perspective. Wrapping TritonGELU.apply(x) in something as simple as 2 * z + 1 reproduces the exact same grad_output = 2 this chapter's predecessor had to construct by hand, except now it happens automatically, as a direct and unavoidable consequence of the surrounding code.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Chapter 16's test This chapter's chain Expression z = TritonGELU.apply(x); z.backward(grad_output) z = TritonGELU.apply(x); w = 2*z + 1; loss = w.sum(); loss.backward() How grad_output at TritonGELU's node is chosen Constructed explicitly by the test, as a stand-in for "whatever comes next" Computed automatically by autograd, as d(loss)/d(w) * d(w)/d(z) = 1 * 2 = 2, uniformly Purpose Isolate and directly control the one input a backward cares about Show that ordinary, unremarkable surrounding code produces exactly this kind of grad_output on its own

docs.title: Worked Example 17.1.1: reading the real grad_output off a chained expression
docs.text:
z = TritonGELU.apply(x)
z.register_hook(lambda grad: captured_grad_output.setdefault("z", grad.clone()))
w = 2 * z + 1
loss = w.sum()
loss.backward()

register_hook runs a callback the moment autograd computes the gradient flowing into z — exactly the grad_output that TritonGELU.backward receives as its argument. On six random values, genuinely captured:

grad_output that arrived at TritonGELU's node (dL/dz): tensor([2., 2., 2., 2., 2., 2.])
x.grad allclose to oracle? True

Uniformly 2.0, matching d(2z+1)/dz = 2 exactly — and x.grad still agrees with computing the entire chain (gelu, then 2*+1, then .sum()) through PyTorch's own autograd from end to end.

docs.title: Worked Example 17.1.2: the chain-rule bug, now surfacing without any hand-constructed input
docs.text:
Reusing Chapter 16's buggy kernel (gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule, which stores the local derivative directly and never multiplies by grad_output) inside this exact same chain, with no modification to the test beyond swapping which kernel backward calls:

buggy chain x.grad:   tensor([ 1.0212,  0.6381,  0.5708,  0.0669,  0.5368, -0.1285])
correct chain x.grad: tensor([ 2.0424,  1.2762,  1.1416,  0.1338,  1.0736, -0.2569])
buggy chain matches oracle? False

The correct chain's gradient is exactly double the buggy chain's — the missing factor of 2 from 2*z+1's own derivative, dropped silently because the buggy kernel never looked at grad_output at all. Nobody had to construct a special test to expose this; it is the default behavior of the single most ordinary way to use a custom autograd op — wrapping it in more arithmetic.

docs.title: ASCII Diagram
docs.text:
FORWARD:    x --[TritonGELU]--> z --[* 2, + 1]--> w --[.sum()]--> loss

BACKWARD (right to left):
  loss:            grad = 1                      (d(loss)/d(loss))
  w:               grad = 1                      (d(sum)/d(each element of w) = 1)
  z:               grad = 1 * 2 = 2               (d(w)/d(z) = 2, chained through)
  x:  TritonGELU.backward(grad_output=2) --> grad_output * (cdf + x*pdf)

  The "2" arriving at TritonGELU is not a special test value --
  it is exactly what "2*z+1" downstream produces, automatically.

[COMMON TRAP] Testing a custom backward only via .sum().backward() tests exactly one input value for grad_output: uniform 1s. That is the one case in which "forgot to multiply by grad_output" and "multiplied by grad_output" produce identical results. Any real use of the op — scaling it, combining it with another tensor, feeding it into a further layer — hands backward a grad_output that is not uniformly 1, and a chain-rule bug invisible in isolation becomes visible the instant the op is actually used the way it's meant to be used.

docs.title: 17.2 [FOUNDATIONAL] Reading the Graph: Traversal Order and next_functions
Intuition
docs.text:
.grad_fn isn't just a label confirming that autograd is tracking a tensor — it's a real, inspectable node in a real graph, and PyTorch exposes the graph's actual structure through it. Each grad_fn object has a .next_functions attribute: a tuple of (function, input_index) pairs pointing to whatever produced its inputs. Following those pointers backward from a loss tensor's .grad_fn, one hop at a time, reconstructs the entire computation graph exactly as autograd itself will walk it — because that walk, in reverse topological order starting from the loss, is precisely how .backward() decides what to call and when.

"Reverse topological order" has a very concrete meaning for a simple chain: if the forward pass ran operation A and then operation B (B's input is A's output), the backward pass calls B's backward first, then A's — the exact reverse of the order the forward operations executed in. This isn't a coincidence or an implementation detail; it's required by the chain rule itself, since A's backward needs a grad_output value that can only be produced by first running B's backward.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Tool What it shows tensor.grad_fn The Function node that produced this tensor, or None for a leaf or a tensor with requires_grad=False tensor.grad_fn.next_functions A tuple of (function, input_index) pointing to the node(s) that produced this node's inputs — None in place of a function marks a leaf with requires_grad=False AccumulateGrad The special node representing "write into .grad on a leaf tensor" — appears in next_functions wherever a graph edge terminates at an original input rather than another operation tensor.register_hook(fn) Runs fn(grad) the moment autograd computes the gradient arriving at this tensor — used in this chapter to observe values that Chapter 16 could only infer indirectly

docs.title: Worked Example 17.2.1: two chained custom ops, TritonGELU then TritonSquare
docs.text:
z = TritonGELU.apply(x)      # forward: GELU runs first
y = TritonSquare.apply(z)    # forward: square runs second
loss = y.sum()
loss.backward()

Genuinely captured, printing .grad_fn and .grad_fn.next_functions before calling .backward(), and the actual order backward methods were invoked (via a shared list each backward appends its own name to):

y.grad_fn: <torch.autograd.function.TritonSquareBackward object at 0x7ff966b4b020>
y.grad_fn.next_functions: ((<torch.autograd.function.TritonGELUBackward object at 0x7ff966b4acf0>, 0),)
z.grad_fn: <torch.autograd.function.TritonGELUBackward object at 0x7ff966b4acf0>
z.grad_fn.next_functions: ((<AccumulateGrad object at 0x7ff9669ef280>, 0),)
backward call order: ['TritonSquare.backward', 'TritonGELU.backward']
x.grad allclose to oracle? True

y's node points directly at z's node (the same TritonGELUBackward object, confirmed by the matching memory address) — exactly the edge the forward pass created by feeding z into TritonSquare.apply. z's node, in turn, points at an AccumulateGrad node, because z's input, x, is a leaf. And the actual call order is TritonSquare first, TritonGELU second — the reverse of TritonGELU, then TritonSquare in the forward pass — because TritonGELU.backward cannot run until it has a grad_output, and the only source of that value is TritonSquare.backward finishing first.

docs.title: ASCII Diagram
docs.text:
FORWARD:   x --[TritonGELU]--> z --[TritonSquare]--> y --[.sum()]--> loss

GRAPH (as .grad_fn.next_functions actually reports it):

  loss.grad_fn
       |
       v
  y.grad_fn = TritonSquareBackward
       | .next_functions[0][0]
       v
  z.grad_fn = TritonGELUBackward
       | .next_functions[0][0]
       v
  AccumulateGrad   (writes the final result into x.grad)

BACKWARD CALL ORDER:  TritonSquareBackward  -->  TritonGELUBackward  -->  AccumulateGrad
                       (called 1st)               (called 2nd)            (writes x.grad)

[COMMON TRAP] It's easy to assume backward runs in the same order the code was written, left to right. It runs in the reverse of the order the forward operations actually executed, which is why TritonSquare.backward — the second line of forward code — is the first backward method called. For a straight-line chain this is simple to predict; Section 17.3 shows why it gets more subtle the moment a single value feeds two different downstream computations.

docs.title: 17.3 [FOUNDATIONAL] Fan-In: How grad_output Is Assembled When a Value Is Used More Than Once
Intuition
docs.text:
Nothing so far has required a value to be used more than once. But it is completely ordinary for one tensor to feed into two different downstream computations — the same hidden layer's output might be used both for a prediction loss and for a regularization term, for instance. When that happens, TritonGELU's output z has two consumers, each independently computing its own contribution to d(loss)/dz. Autograd's rule for this is simple to state and easy to verify directly: sum every consumer's contribution together, and call the producer's backward exactly once, with that single, already-summed grad_output — never once per consumer.

This is the mechanism Chapter 16's grad_output — treated, until now, as an opaque input handed down from "whatever's next" — is actually built from in general: not necessarily one clean derivative from one neighboring operation, but potentially a sum across every path through the graph that eventually reaches this node. A custom backward that assumed grad_output always reflects a single, clean use of its output would be making an assumption autograd never promised to keep.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Usage pattern grad_output arriving at the producer's backward Number of times backward is called z used once: loss = z.sum() d(loss)/dz, from that one consumer Once z used twice, same op: loss = z.sum() + z.sum() Sum of both d(...)/dz contributions (1 + 1 = 2, uniformly) Once — not twice z used twice, different ops: loss = (2*z).sum() + (3*z).sum() Sum of both contributions (2 + 3 = 5, uniformly) Once

docs.title: Worked Example 17.3.1: the same value summed twice into the loss
docs.text:
z = TritonGELU.apply(x)
loss = z.sum() + z.sum()
loss.backward()

Genuinely captured, comparing against the single-use case and counting how many times TritonGELU.backward actually ran:

used once  -> grad_output at TritonGELU.backward: tensor([1., 1., 1., 1.])
used twice -> grad_output at TritonGELU.backward: tensor([2., 2., 2., 2.])
(single call to backward, already summed -- not called twice)
number of times TritonGELU.backward was called: 1
x2.grad allclose to oracle? True

Using z twice doubles grad_output uniformly, exactly as d(z.sum() + z.sum())/dz = 1 + 1 = 2 predicts — and, critically, TritonGELU.backward is called exactly once, with that pre-summed value, not twice with a 1 each time.

docs.title: Worked Example 17.3.2: two different consumers with different coefficients
docs.text:
z = TritonGELU.apply(x)
loss = (2 * z).sum() + (3 * z).sum()
loss.backward()

Genuinely captured:

grad_output at TritonGELU.backward (expect uniformly 5.0): tensor([5., 5., 5., 5.])
x3.grad allclose to oracle? True

5.0 is exactly 2 + 3 — the sum of each consumer's own local derivative with respect to z, assembled by autograd before TritonGELU.backward is ever invoked, and delivered as one ordinary-looking grad_output tensor indistinguishable, from TritonGELU.backward's point of view, from a single consumer that happened to produce a coefficient of 5.

docs.title: ASCII Diagram
docs.text:
FORWARD:        x --[TritonGELU]--> z --+--[* 2]--> --[.sum()]--\
                                          |                       +--> loss
                                          +--[* 3]--> --[.sum()]--/

BACKWARD (fan-in):        d(loss)/dz via the "*2" path  =  2
                           d(loss)/dz via the "*3" path  =  3
                           ---------------------------------
                           SUMMED before TritonGELU.backward runs = 5

                           TritonGELU.backward(grad_output=[5,5,5,5])
                           <-- called exactly ONCE, not once per path

[COMMON TRAP] A custom backward must never assume the grad_output it receives reflects only one "clean" use of its output — by the time backward is called, autograd has already summed every consumer's contribution into that single tensor, and there is no way for backward to tell, from grad_output alone, whether it came from one consumer or ten. Writing a backward that tries to special-case "the first time I'm called" or assumes a specific consumer produced this value is building on a guarantee autograd does not make; the only safe assumption is that grad_output is some correctly-summed gradient, from however many paths actually exist.

docs.text: The three files below build up the chapter in order: chaining TritonGELU inside ordinary arithmetic and exposing the chain-rule bug without a hand-constructed input (17.1), inspecting the graph structure and backward call order across two chained custom ops (17.2), and fan-in accumulation across single and multiple consumers (17.3) — plus one standalone file combining all three with a single documented Expected Output block.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def gelu_forward_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    out = x * cdf
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, out, mask=mask)


@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)


@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, d_gelu, mask=mask)  # BUG: never multiplied by grad_out


def triton_gelu_forward(x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_forward_kernel[grid](x, out, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return out


def _launch_bwd(kernel, grad_output, x, BLOCK=1024):
    grad_input = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    kernel[grid](grad_output, x, grad_input, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return grad_input


class TritonGELU(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        out = triton_gelu_forward(x)
        ctx.save_for_backward(x)
        return out

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        x, = ctx.saved_tensors
        return _launch_bwd(gelu_backward_kernel, grad_output.contiguous(), x)


class TritonGELUBuggy(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        out = triton_gelu_forward(x)
        ctx.save_for_backward(x)
        return out

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        x, = ctx.saved_tensors
        return _launch_bwd(gelu_backward_kernel_buggy_no_chain_rule, grad_output.contiguous(), x)


def section_17_1():
    print("=== Section 17.1: TritonGELU chained inside w = 2*z + 1, loss = w.sum() ===")
    torch.manual_seed(3)
    x = torch.randn(6, requires_grad=True)

    captured_grad_output = {}
    z = TritonGELU.apply(x)
    z.register_hook(lambda grad: captured_grad_output.setdefault("z", grad.clone()))
    w = 2 * z + 1
    loss = w.sum()
    loss.backward()

    print("grad_output that arrived at TritonGELU's node (dL/dz):", captured_grad_output["z"])

    x_oracle = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
    (2 * z_oracle + 1).sum().backward()
    print("x.grad allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(x.grad, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))

    print()
    print("=== Section 17.1: the buggy kernel inside the SAME chain, no hand-injected grad_output ===")
    x2 = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z2 = TritonGELUBuggy.apply(x2)
    loss2 = (2 * z2 + 1).sum()
    loss2.backward()
    print("buggy chain matches oracle?", torch.allclose(x2.grad, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    section_17_1()

@triton.jit
def gelu_backward_kernel(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):

    mask = offsets < n
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    grad_out = tl.load(grad_out_ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)
    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)
    d_gelu = cdf + x * pdf
    grad_in = grad_out * d_gelu
    tl.store(grad_in_ptr + offsets, grad_in, mask=mask)


def triton_gelu_forward(x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    out = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_forward_kernel[grid](x, out, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return out


def triton_gelu_backward(grad_output, x, BLOCK=1024):
    x = x.contiguous()
    grad_output = grad_output.contiguous()
    grad_input = torch.empty_like(x)
    n = x.numel()
    grid = (triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)
    gelu_backward_kernel[grid](grad_output, x, grad_input, n, BLOCK=BLOCK)
    return grad_input


captured = []


class TritonGELU(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, x):
        out = triton_gelu_forward(x)
        ctx.save_for_backward(x)
        return out

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        captured.append(grad_output.clone())
        x, = ctx.saved_tensors
        return triton_gelu_backward(grad_output.contiguous(), x)

    print("=== Section 17.3: z used once vs. z used twice (same op) ===")
    torch.manual_seed(5)
    x1 = torch.randn(4, requires_grad=True)

    captured.clear()
    z1 = TritonGELU.apply(x1)
    z1.sum().backward()
    print("used once  -> grad_output:", captured[-1])

    captured.clear()
    x2 = x1.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z2 = TritonGELU.apply(x2)
    (z2.sum() + z2.sum()).backward()
    print("used twice -> grad_output:", captured[-1])
    print("number of times backward was called:", len(captured))

    captured.clear()
    x3 = x1.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z3 = TritonGELU.apply(x3)
    ((2 * z3).sum() + (3 * z3).sum()).backward()
    print("grad_output (expect uniformly 5.0):", captured[-1])

    x_oracle2 = x1.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z_oracle2 = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle2, approximate="none")

    print("x3.grad allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(x3.grad, x_oracle2.grad, atol=1e-5))

Chapter 17 standalone: chaining a custom autograd.Function inside ordinary
PyTorch expressions, reading the resulting graph structure directly, and
confirming how grad_output is assembled when a value has more than one
consumer.

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Shared kernels: GELU forward/backward (correct and buggy), and square
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@triton.jit
def gelu_forward_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)

def gelu_backward_kernel(grad_out_ptr, x_ptr, grad_in_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):

    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))
    pdf = SQRT_2PI_INV * tl.exp(-0.5 * x * x)

    SQRT_2_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.7071067811865476
    SQRT_2PI_INV: tl.constexpr = 0.3989422804014327
    cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + tl.math.erf(x * SQRT_2_INV))

@triton.jit
def square_forward_kernel(x_ptr, out_ptr, n, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):

    torch.manual_seed(3)

    hook_captured = {}

    x2 = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z2 = TritonGELUBuggy.apply(x2)

def section_17_2():
    print()
    print("=== Section 17.2: graph structure and backward call order ===")
    torch.manual_seed(4)
    x = torch.randn(4, requires_grad=True)
    z = TritonGELU.apply(x)
    y = TritonSquare.apply(z)

    print("y.grad_fn is TritonSquareBackward?", "TritonSquareBackward" in str(y.grad_fn))
    print("z.grad_fn is TritonGELUBackward?  ", "TritonGELUBackward" in str(z.grad_fn))
    print("y.grad_fn.next_functions[0][0] is z.grad_fn?",
          y.grad_fn.next_functions[0][0] is z.grad_fn)

    call_order.clear()
    y.sum().backward()
    print("backward call order:", call_order)

    x_oracle = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
    (z_oracle * z_oracle).sum().backward()
    print("x.grad allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(x.grad, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))


def section_17_3():
    print()
    print("=== Section 17.3: fan-in accumulation ===")
    torch.manual_seed(5)
    x1 = torch.randn(4, requires_grad=True)

    captured_grads.clear()
    z1 = TritonGELU.apply(x1)
    z1.sum().backward()
    print("used once  -> grad_output:", captured_grads[-1])

    captured_grads.clear()
    x2 = x1.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z2 = TritonGELU.apply(x2)
    (z2.sum() + z2.sum()).backward()
    print("used twice -> grad_output:", captured_grads[-1], " (backward called", len(captured_grads), "time(s))")

    captured_grads.clear()
    x3 = x1.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z3 = TritonGELU.apply(x3)
    ((2 * z3).sum() + (3 * z3).sum()).backward()
    print("two different consumers (2x + 3x) -> grad_output:", captured_grads[-1])

    x_oracle = x1.detach().clone().requires_grad_(True)
    z_oracle = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x_oracle, approximate="none")
    ((2 * z_oracle).sum() + (3 * z_oracle).sum()).backward()
    print("x3.grad allclose to oracle?", torch.allclose(x3.grad, x_oracle.grad, atol=1e-5))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    section_17_1()
    section_17_2()
    section_17_3()
